summary: Specifies the frame format for sending IPv6 packets over Ethernet and how link-local addresses are formed there. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard. It was replaced by RFC 2464.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1972 explains how Ethernet carries IPv6 packets and how an Ethernet interface forms a link-local IPv6 address. It also defines how IPv6 addresses map to Ethernet addresses; RFC 2464 later replaced this memo.

subtitle: The frame and address rules for sending IPv6 packets over Ethernet.

tldr.problem: IPv6 needed rules for carrying its packets over Ethernet and forming Ethernet interface addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The memo specifies the Ethernet type code, a default MTU, link-local address formation, and mappings between IPv6 and Ethernet addresses.

sections.title: IPv6 Packets in Ethernet Frames
sections.content:
IPv6 packets use standard Ethernet frames. The Ethernet header contains destination and source Ethernet addresses and a type code of 86DD hexadecimal to identify IPv6. The data field contains the IPv6 header followed by its payload, with padding possible to meet Ethernet's minimum frame size.

The default MTU for IPv6 packets on Ethernet is 1500 octets. A node can use a smaller value from a Router Advertisement or from manual configuration. It must ignore an advertised value larger than 1500 or larger than a manually configured value below 1500.
sections.plainLanguage: An Ethernet frame labels its contents with the type code 86DD when it carries IPv6. The default packet limit is 1500 octets, and a router or local setting can make it smaller.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses and Ethernet Mapping
sections.content:
For stateless address autoconfiguration, the Ethernet interface's address token is its built-in 48-bit IEEE 802 address, in the same octet order used in an Ethernet frame. The link-local IPv6 address is formed by appending that address to the 80-bit prefix FE80::.

Neighbor Discovery link-layer address options carry an Ethernet address and use a length of 1 in units of 8 octets. For IPv6 multicast, the Ethernet multicast address starts with the two octets 33 33 and ends with the last four octets of the IPv6 multicast destination.
sections.plainLanguage: An Ethernet interface forms its link-local address from the prefix FE80:: and its built-in Ethernet address. Multicast IPv6 destinations map to Ethernet addresses beginning with 33 33.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content: The memo says security issues are not discussed. It defines the Ethernet transmission method and address mappings for IPv6 in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security issues. RFC 2464 later obsoleted this specification.
